chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 65 — Noah’s Cry and Enoch’s Flood Warning
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language text responsibly available for this chapter. No extant Aramaic or Greek wording has been identified for this Noahic unit within the Parables. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, is the translation base for all twelve verses: Noah's fear as the earth sinks, his threefold cry to his grandfather Enoch, the indictment of destructive angelic secrets and metalworking, and the promise that Noah and his righteous seed will be preserved. The witness's abrupt first-person Noahic voice, difficult list of secret arts, and ancient account of metals from the earth are retained without modernizing their mechanism. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: In those days Noah saw that the earth had sunk down and that its destruction was near.
verses.study: Noah recognizes the physical world bending toward catastrophe. The visible sinking of the earth corresponds to the moral collapse explained later in the chapter.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:11–13 — a corrupted earth approaches destruction
Psalm 46:2 — the earth can give way beneath human security

verses.text: He lifted his feet from there, went to the extremities of the earth, and cried out to his grandfather Enoch. Noah said three times with a bitter voice, ‘Hear me! Hear me! Hear me!’
verses.study: The threefold cry expresses urgent helplessness. Noah seeks the ancestor associated with heavenly revelation because ordinary observation cannot explain what the earth is becoming.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:22–24 — Enoch walks with God and is taken
Psalm 55:2–5 — fear and anguish drive a bitter cry for attention

verses.text: He said to him, ‘Tell me what is happening upon the earth, for the earth is laboring and shaking like this. Perhaps I will perish together with it.’
verses.study: Noah does not assume personal exemption. He asks for understanding while confessing that he may share the world's destruction.
crossReferences: Jeremiah 4:23–26 — the land trembles and creation appears undone
Romans 8:22 — creation groans together in labor pains

verses.text: After that moment a great disturbance arose upon the earth, a voice was heard from heaven, and I fell upon my face.
verses.study: Earthly upheaval is answered by a heavenly voice. Noah's fall shows that the requested explanation arrives with an authority he cannot meet standing.
crossReferences: Exodus 19:18–19 — the mountain shakes as the heavenly voice answers
Daniel 10:9 — the recipient of revelation falls before the voice

verses.text: My grandfather Enoch came and stood beside me. He said to me, ‘Why did you cry to me with a bitter cry and weeping?’
verses.study: Enoch's presence turns Noah's distant appeal into direct instruction. The question invites Noah's fear to be interpreted rather than dismissed.
crossReferences: Genesis 21:17 — a heavenly response asks why the distressed one weeps
Acts 9:4–6 — a heavenly encounter addresses the reason for a human cry

verses.text: ‘A command has gone out from the presence of the Lord against those who dwell upon the dry ground, that their end should come. For they learned all the hidden things of the angels, all the violence of the satans, every concealed power, the power of those who practice sorcery, the power of enchantments, and the power of those who cast images for all the earth.’
verses.study: The earth's destruction is traced to weaponized hidden knowledge. Spiritual violence, sorcery and image-making have become systems spread across the inhabited world.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:5, 11–13 — pervasive evil and violence precede the flood
1 Enoch 8:1–3 — forbidden arts spread corruption among humanity
Acts 19:18–20 — destructive magical practices are exposed and renounced

verses.text: ‘They learned how silver is produced from the dust of the earth and how molten metal comes to be upon the earth. For lead and tin are not produced from the earth like the first metals; a spring produces them, and an angel stands within it, and that angel is preeminent.’
verses.study: The witness preserves an ancient account of metal origins and angelic custody. Its theological claim is that technical power entered a corrupt network of disclosed secrets, not that the passage offers modern geology.
crossReferences: Job 28:1–11 — humans mine silver and search earth's hidden depths
Ezekiel 22:18–22 — metals and smelting become imagery for moral judgment

verses.text: After this my grandfather Enoch took me by his hand, raised me, and said to me, ‘Go, for I have asked the Lord of Spirits about this disturbance upon the earth.’
verses.study: Enoch both steadies Noah and reports intercession. The explanation is grounded in an answer sought from the Lord of Spirits.
crossReferences: Daniel 10:10–12 — a heavenly hand raises the seer and reports that his words were heard
James 1:5 — wisdom is sought from God when understanding is lacking

verses.text: ‘He said to me, “Because of their unrighteousness, their judgment has been completed, and it will no longer be withheld before Me. Because of the months in which they investigated and learned that the earth and those who dwell upon it would be destroyed, their judgment is fixed.”’
verses.study: The guilty used time and inquiry to deepen corrupt knowledge rather than turn back. Judgment is described as completed because their chosen course has reached fullness.
crossReferences: Genesis 15:16 — wrongdoing reaches a completed measure before judgment
Romans 2:5 — persistent hardness stores up judgment

verses.text: ‘“For them there will be no return forever, because they revealed what was hidden and have been condemned. But as for you, my son, the Lord of Spirits knows that you are pure and good, apart from this reproach concerning hidden things.”’
verses.study: Noah is distinguished not by ignorance of the warning but by freedom from the corrupt disclosure that caused ruin. The Lord knows his integrity amid a condemned generation.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:8–9 — Noah is found righteous and blameless in his generation
2 Peter 2:5 — Noah is preserved as a herald of righteousness

verses.text: ‘“He has established your name among the holy and will preserve you from those who dwell upon the dry ground. He has established your seed in righteousness for kingship and great glory.”’
verses.study: Preservation extends into vocation and descendants. Noah's name and seed are secured for righteousness rather than merely for biological survival.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:1, 8–11 — Noah's family receives blessing and covenant after the flood
Isaiah 54:9–10 — the covenant associated with Noah supports enduring mercy

verses.text: ‘“From your seed a spring of righteous and holy people will go forth, and their number will be without end forever.”’
verses.study: The chapter closes with life flowing from preserved seed like a spring. The flood warning is therefore joined to a future multitude marked by righteousness and holiness.
crossReferences: Isaiah 44:3–4 — blessing poured on descendants makes them spring up like plants by water
Revelation 7:9 — an innumerable holy multitude stands before God

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 65 speaks in Noah's first person and identifies Enoch as his grandfather, making its Noahic voice explicit. Noah sees the earth's collapse, fears sharing its fate and cries three times for revealed understanding.

Enoch explains that the flood judgment answers the spread of corrupt heavenly secrets. Violence, sorcery, enchantments, images and technical mastery have been turned into instruments of worldwide sin.

The account of metals belongs to the witness's ancient cosmology and is preserved as such. Its enduring theological concern is responsibility for knowledge: discovery without righteousness can magnify destruction.
Noah is known as pure from this reproach and is preserved with a future. His seed becomes a spring of righteous and holy people, so judgment of corruption is joined to covenantal continuity.

crossReferences: Genesis 6:5–13 — corruption, violence and Noah's righteousness
Genesis 9:8–11 — covenant with Noah and his descendants
1 Enoch 8:1–3 — forbidden arts disclosed by the Watchers
Job 28:1–11 — mining and the search for hidden things
2 Peter 2:5 — Noah preserved as a herald of righteousness
